title: European Researchers Say Big Tech Is Blocking Access to Their Data
gist: European disinformation researchers legally entitled to platform data under the EU's Digital Services Act say TikTok, X, and Meta obstruct access through security requirements universities cannot meet, daily API caps, narrow readings of 'systemic risk', and litigation — leaving events like the annulled Romanian presidential first round unstudied in real time. The DSA40 Collaboratory tracks 46 applications (20 approved, 14 rejected), X was fined €120 million in December 2025 partly over researcher-access barriers and has now agreed a remediation plan it must implement within six months.

themes.theme: Romania as the cost of denied access

insights.claim: TikTok accounts that had spent years posting about manicures or fashion abruptly began promoting little-known Romanian politician Calin Georgescu, whose posts drew 120 million views before the November 2024 vote as he went from single-digit polling to winning the first round with 23 percent.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: A documented case where repurposed lifestyle accounts moved a national election outcome — the template for platform-mediated political risk in any EU vote.
insights.quote: His posts, espousing hard-line views on immigration and anti-Semitic tropes, were viewed 120 million times before the vote.
insights.locator: Opening — 'In the final weeks before Romania’s presidential vote'

insights.claim: Maastricht University's Adriana Iamnitchi applied for TikTok API access under the DSA on October 28, 2025 to study how pro-Georgescu content was monetized through hidden-influencer marketing and livestreamed political content, and was denied on grounds she had not proved she was an established researcher, explained commercial interests, or met security requirements.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: Shows the rejection criteria are subjective enough to block a chaired academic — the practical bar, not the statutory right, is what governs access.
insights.quote: TikTok said they had failed to prove they were established researchers or to explain their commercial interests or to meet security requirements
insights.locator: 'On October 28, 2025, a month before Georgescu won the first round'

insights.claim: Two months after denying the researchers' request, TikTok itself flagged 116k potentially compromised accounts and acted against more than 27,000 fake accounts in a coordinated network run by a third-party fake engagement vendor promoting Georgescu and the AUR party, while saying it did not know who operated the network or where it originated.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
entities: Alliance for the Union of Romanians
insights.so_what: The platform confirmed the manipulation it had refused to let outsiders study, and could not attribute it — the strongest argument that independent access adds capability the platform lacks.
insights.quote: TikTok said it did not know who operated the network or where it originated.
insights.locator: 'But two month’s later, TikTok flagged 116k accounts'

insights.claim: Romania annulled the first round, Georgescu was barred from running again, and independent former Bucharest mayor Nicușor Dan beat AUR's George Simion in the May 2025 runoff, with declassified Romanian intelligence saying Georgescu benefited from preferential treatment by TikTok and that Russia had allegedly coordinated the campaign.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: A state-attributed influence operation that forced an annulled election sets the political precondition for harder EU enforcement against platforms.
insights.quote: Declassified Romanian intelligence showed he “benefited” from massive exposure and preferential treatment by TikTok and that Russia had allegedly coordinated the online campaign to elect Georgescu.
insights.locator: 'Declassified Romanian intelligence showed'

insights.claim: Iamnitchi believes her team could have identified who created and profited from the pro-Georgescu content had they obtained the data, meaning the attribution gap is a direct consequence of the access denial rather than a methodological limit.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: Frames data access as the binding constraint on election-integrity forensics — the lever regulators can actually pull.
insights.quote: “When you need data to investigate that impact, and that data is privately held, it can become practically impossible to research this space.”
insights.locator: 'Iamnitchi believes her team might have been able to identify'

themes.theme: How access is throttled in practice

insights.claim: The obstruction operates through implementation rather than statute: the DSA was broadened last year to increase researcher access, but researchers say the problem is how platforms implement the law, not the scope of the law itself.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: Legislative expansion alone won't move the needle — watch implementing standards, vetting rules, and enforcement actions as the real signal on compliance cost.
insights.quote: Last year the law was broadened to increase researcher access, but it’s the implementation not the scope of the law itself that researchers say is the issue.
insights.locator: 'Iamnitchi is one of several misinformation researchers'

insights.claim: Most DSA data-access application forms require data to be stored on infrastructure that cannot be compromised — such as a machine physically disconnected from the internet — a resource most universities lack, making the security requirement a de facto exclusion.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: Compliance friction disguised as security is the durable moat; any EU standardization of vetting directly lowers that moat and raises platform data-exposure.
insights.quote: most require data to be stored on infrastructure that cannot be compromised—such as a machine physically disconnected from the internet—a resource most universities lack
insights.locator: 'Application forms differ by platform'

insights.claim: Platforms retired public research tools and replaced them with gated or paid substitutes — Meta shut CrowdTangle in favor of content libraries and X paywalled its API at hundreds of dollars a month, per DRI research officer Duncan Allen.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: API monetization and tool retirement converted a free public-research channel into a revenue and control point — the thing DSA enforcement is now trying to unwind.
insights.quote: social media companies shut down public access tools like Meta’s CrowdTangle and replaced them with content libraries, or, like X, paywalled their API data, forcing academics to pay “hundreds of dollars a month,”
insights.locator: 'In recent years, social media companies shut down public access tools'

insights.claim: TikTok caps how many posts a researcher account can pull each day, which Duncan Allen says makes it impossible to study anything at scale even when access is granted.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: Rate limits are the second gate after approval — approval statistics alone overstate real access.
insights.quote: Others, like TikTok, cap how many posts any researcher account can pull each day, which Allen said can make it “impossible to study anything at scale.”
insights.locator: 'Others, like TikTok, cap how many posts'

insights.claim: Even approved researchers cannot guarantee data quality: API data is often difficult for a colleague to reproduce, so results cannot be independently checked for errors, which Iamnitchi calls a basic requirement of science.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: Non-reproducible platform data undermines the evidentiary base regulators and courts will rely on — a weakness platforms can exploit in appeals.
insights.quote: “there's no guarantee that the data is good,”
insights.locator: 'Even for researchers who secure approval'

insights.claim: Of 46 DSA applications tracked by the German DSA40 Collaboratory, 20 were approved and 14 rejected, with sharply divergent platform behavior: TikTok approved 11 of 13 applications while X rejected 11 of 23.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: Platform-level approval spreads identify who is most exposed to EU enforcement — X is the outlier and drew the first penalty.
insights.quote: DSA40 data shows that of 46 tracked applications, 20 were approved and 14 rejected.
insights.locator: 'DSA40 data shows that of 46 tracked applications'

insights.claim: The tracked rejection rate understates reality because the DSA40 tracker relies on voluntary reporting, per coordinator L. K. Seiling — so published approval statistics are a floor, not an estimate.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: Treat platform-friendly access metrics skeptically; the measurement infrastructure itself is incomplete.
insights.quote: The true rejection rate is likely higher because the tracker relies on voluntary reporting, Seiling said.
insights.locator: 'The true rejection rate is likely higher'

insights.claim: Seiling argues data access as currently configured actively disincentivizes researchers from using the legal pathway, meaning the DSA channel competes badly against scraping and informal methods.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: If the statutory route is worse than the workaround, compliance metrics will look fine while research output stays flat — regulators must fix incentives, not just rights.
insights.quote: “There's no structured advantage for researchers to use this pathway,” Seiling said. “Data access as it’s set up right now tries to disincentivize researchers.”
insights.locator: 'There's no structured advantage for researchers'

insights.claim: Scraping is the main workaround but cannot capture an account's complete follower list, which makes coordinated disinformation networks difficult to map — the exact analysis that election-integrity work requires.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: Identifies follower-graph data as the specific asset with research value — which is why the new nonpublic-data provisions matter more than volume caps.
insights.quote: It cannot capture an account’s complete follower list, making coordinated disinformation networks difficult to map.
insights.locator: 'There are few workarounds'

insights.claim: TikTok says it has given more than 1,500 research teams access to its tools, approved 130 EU applications in the second half of last year, and that its 1,000-request daily quota permits pulling up to 100,000 video and comment records or 2 million follower records per day.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: TikTok's numbers are the benchmark platforms will cite against tighter rules — compare them against the DSA40 sample and researcher accounts of usability.
insights.quote: its daily quota of 1,000 API requests lets researchers pull up to 100,000 video and comment records a day, or up to 2 million follower records
insights.locator: 'A TikTok spokesperson told WIRED'

insights.claim: TikTok considers its research tools DSA-compliant but says it would welcome further public guidance, signaling the ambiguity of the standard is itself part of the platform's defense.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: Regulatory ambiguity is the current equilibrium; the EU's new vetting standard is the event that removes the excuse.
insights.quote: TikTok said it considers its research tools compliant with the DSA but “would welcome further public guidance.”
insights.locator: 'TikTok said it considers its research tools compliant'

insights.claim: Meta argues CrowdTangle covered only a fraction of its public data and that the Meta Content Library and API replacing it are the most comprehensive research tools to date, spanning Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp Channels, and Threads with robust privacy protections.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: Meta's coverage-breadth defense sets up a fight over data quality and usability rather than volume — where the EU has already signaled skepticism.
insights.quote: the Meta Content Library and API that replaced it are “the most comprehensive research tools to date.”
insights.locator: 'A Meta spokesperson said CrowdTangle covered only a fraction'

themes.theme: Litigation and the first DSA penalty

insights.claim: Democracy Reporting International and the Society for Civil Rights applied for X API access in April 2024 to study political discourse before Germany's federal election, were rejected in November, sued in February 2025, and won a ruling that X should have granted access.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: Courts will enforce DSA access rights, but the ten-month application-to-ruling lag means litigation cannot deliver data in time for the election being studied.
insights.quote: The court ruled X should have granted access, in what DRI believed could become a precedent-setting case.
insights.locator: 'One way to challenge a rejected request is to take the platforms to court'

insights.claim: DRI's follow-on case over X's denial of data for Hungary's election nearly collapsed when a Berlin court ruled the researchers should have sued in Ireland where X is based, before DRI won on appeal — showing jurisdiction is a live obstruction tactic under EU law.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: Forum shopping toward Ireland raises the cost of every enforcement action against platforms domiciled there — a structural advantage worth monitoring in EU tech litigation.
insights.quote: “EU law is still not uniformly applied,”
insights.locator: 'That case nearly collapsed when a Berlin court ruled'

insights.claim: The European Commission imposed its first-ever DSA penalty in December 2025, fining X €120 million ($137 million) partly for creating unnecessary barriers to researcher access that effectively undermine research into risks in the EU.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: Establishes a price for researcher-access obstruction and a precedent other platforms must now underwrite against.
insights.quote: the European Commission imposed its first DSA penalty, fining X €120 million ($137 million) partly for creating “unnecessary barriers” to researcher access
insights.locator: 'In December 2025, the European Commission imposed its first DSA penalty'

insights.claim: X appealed on February 20, 2026, calling the Commission's investigation incomplete and superficial and accusing the EU of systemic breaches of rights of defence and basic due process requirements.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: A due-process challenge to the first DSA fine is the test case for whether the regime's penalties survive judicial review.
insights.quote: accusing the EU of “systemic breaches of rights of defence and basic due process requirements.”
insights.locator: 'On February 20, 2026, X appealed'

insights.claim: The Commission accepted an X action plan to fix researcher screening, provide data free of charge, cut processing times, and lift restrictions on data scraping, with six months for X to implement the changes.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: A dated, checkable compliance milestone — free data plus lifted scraping limits at X is a concrete change in the platform-data landscape within six months.
insights.quote: Last week, the commission accepted X’s action plan to fix the researcher screening process, provide data free of charge, cut processing times, and lift restrictions on data scraping.
insights.locator: 'Last week, the commission accepted X’s action plan'

themes.theme: What changes next under EU rules

insights.claim: The EU said in a separate DSA investigation that Meta and TikTok may have put in place burdensome procedures and tools leaving researchers with partial or unreliable data, and started meeting platforms in May to build a new standard for vetting researchers.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: A standardized vetting process would strip out the discretionary rejection lever platforms currently rely on — watch for the standard's publication.
insights.quote: “may have put in place burdensome procedures and tools for researchers to request access to public data,”
insights.locator: 'The EU, having said in another DSA investigation'

insights.claim: The Commission expanded researchers' access to nonpublic platform data late last year to cover risks including illegal content, financial scams, and recommender systems, though researchers say the new provisions have yet to be tested.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: Recommender-system data is the most commercially sensitive asset in scope — the first successful request under these provisions is the milestone to watch.
insights.quote: the commission also expanded researchers’ access to nonpublic platform data to study risks including illegal content, financial scams, and recommender systems
insights.locator: 'Late last year, the commission also expanded'

insights.claim: New nonpublic-data rules could force X to release an account's full follower list, giving disinformation researchers the ability to map which accounts interact or follow one another and how they amplify content, per DRI's Duncan Allen.
insights.speaker: Anna Desmarais
insights.so_what: Compelled follower-graph disclosure would be the single biggest change in coordinated-manipulation detection capability — and the biggest data-moat concession for X.
insights.quote: The new regulations on nonpublic data could force X to release an account’s full follower list.
insights.locator: Final paragraph — 'The new regulations on nonpublic data'
